name: South Central Dinka
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Andersen, Torben. 1987. The phonemic system of Agar Dinka (= South Central Dinka), JALL 9:1-27 — paywalled, not read

new_statements.quote: Dinka is a Western Nilotic language with three contrastive degrees of vowel length, two contrastive voice qualities in vowels, and three contrastive tones. Although to a large extent a monosyllabic language, Dinka has an elaborate morphology. [p. 1] ... In this section I outline the system of phonological contrasts existing in monosyllabic words of Agar Dinka. For more details the reader should see Andersen [1987]. [p. 3] ... There are three contrasting tones: High, Low, and Falling, the latter falling from the level of High to the level of Low. [p. 5] ... Tone is independent of vowel length (and of voice quality and vowel quality), except that the contrast between H and F seems to be neutralized on short vowels. [p. 6]
new_statements.citation: Andersen, Torben. 1992-1994. Morphological stratification in Dinka: On the alternations of voice quality, vowel length and tone in the morphology of transitive verbal roots in a monosyllabic language. Studies in African Linguistics 23(1): 1-63.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Agar (South Central) Dinka is described as a tone language (H, L, F on the single vowel of a largely monosyllabic word) with contrastive vowel length and voice quality; none of Andersen's accessible Agar descriptions (1992, 2017, 2020, 2023, 2025) mentions word stress at all. The only accent-placement remarks come from the two 19th-century Holy Cross mission grammars of the Ciec/Kyec variety: Beltrame 1869 p. 239 says the written accents mark vowel quality/length and that 'where the accent falls the rest of the voice (posa della voce) must also fall', specifying case by case which vowel carries it, his examples all being the last vowel (uen-e, gon-ter, ke-piat p. 241); Mitterrutzner 1866 sec. 15 p. 12 says polysyllabic words without tone marks have all syllables at the same pitch, and p. 20 that in ke- abstract nouns 'der Ton ruht immer auf der letzten Silbe'. No general word-stress rule is stated by any opened source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Beltrame 1869 p. 239 (Italian): 'Ove cade l'accento dovra pur cadere la posa della voce; che se talvolta dovetti accentare piu d'una vocale, nella stessa parola, per determinarne i suoni, dissi pero sempre fra parentesi, su quale vocale deve cadere la posa della voce: p. e. uen-e questo fanciullo; gon-ter da molto tempo (la voce posa sull'ultima vocale).' = 'Where the accent falls, the rest of the voice must also fall; when I had to accent more than one vowel in the same word to fix their sounds, I always said in parentheses on which vowel the rest of the voice must fall, e.g. uen-e this boy; gon-ter long ago (the voice rests on the last vowel).' Mitterrutzner 1866 p. 12 (German): 'Sind die Vokale eines mehrsilbigen Wortes mit keinem Tonzeichen versehen, so gilt die Regel, dass alle Silben die gleiche Tonhoehe haben' = 'If the vowels of a polysyllabic word bear no tone mark, the rule is that all syllables have the same pitch'; p. 20: 'Bei diesen abstrakten Substantiven ruht der Ton immer auf der letzten Silbe' = 'In these (ke-) abstract nouns the accent always rests on the last syllable.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Dinka roots are monosyllabic (Andersen 1992 sec. 2), polysyllables being prefixed/compound forms, which is why stress is not a live category in the modern descriptions. Beltrame and Mitterrutzner describe the Kyec/Ciec (Holy Cross mission) variety in 1860s missionary notation, with 'accento'/'Ton' covering vowel quality, length and pitch as well as prominence; Andersen describes Agar (Rumbek).
new_statements.identity_note: Andersen's papers describe the Agar dialect (Rumbek area), which Glottolog places under South Central Dinka sout2833. Mitterrutzner 1866 and Beltrame 1869 describe the Dinka of the Heiligkreuz/Holy Cross mission among the Kyec (Ciec) tribe at 6 deg 40' N on the west bank of the White Nile (Mitterrutzner pp. XI-XII), i.e. the Ciec variety of South Central Dinka (dialect-level glottocode not verified). Luanyjang/Rek (Remijsen & Manyang 2009, Remijsen & Ladd 2008, Nebel 1948) and Bor (Remijsen 2013, van Urk 2015) materials held under sout2832/sout2834 are other Dinka languages and were not used here.

sources.note: Sec. 2 (pp. 3-6) outlines the phonological contrasts of Agar Dinka: 3 vowel lengths, 2 voice qualities, 3 tones (H, L, F), largely monosyllabic words; refers to Andersen 1987 for detail. Not one occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in the whole article.

sources.citation: Andersen, Torben. 2025. Morphology of intransitive verbs in the Agar dialect of Dinka. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics (online 2025-11-03), CC-BY. doi:10.1515/jall-2025-0041
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 Phonology: ternary tonal contrast (L, H, F; R in some derived forms), vowel length, voice quality; diacritics placed on first vowel symbol. No mention of stress. Reference list names Blum 2023 (Edinburgh PhD, cross-variety Dinka tonal phonology) and Remijsen 2010 (TIE4 slides 'Tone systems of Dinka dialects').

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 (p. 3): monosyllabic root CV(V)(V)C, breathy vs non-breathy vowel, tone low/high/falling in Agar (fn. 3: four tones in some other dialects, citing Remijsen & Ladd 2008). No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Beltrame, Giovanni. 1869. Grammatica della lingua Denka (first instalment). Bollettino della Societa Geografica Italiana 2: 231-249 (continued 1869-70; book edition Roma 1880). archive.org bollettinodella39italgoog
sources.note: Sec. III p. 239: four accents (acute, grave, two circumflexes) mark vowel quality and length, not stress; 'Ove cade l'accento dovra pur cadere la posa della voce'; where more than one vowel is accented he states in parentheses which vowel takes the 'posa della voce' (uen-e 'this boy', gon-ter 'long ago' (la voce posa sull'ultima vocale)); p. 241: 'ke-piat (posa sull'ultima vocale), belta, bonta'. Examples are all final, but no general rule is stated.
